idiom_name: branch?/children/makeNode protocol over plain arrays or objects
implementation_notes: JavaScript's idiom is the generic zipper popularised by clojure.zip: keep nodes as plain data and describe the tree once with a small protocol - is this a branch, what are its children, how is a node with new children built - so one implementation navigates arrays, JSON documents and ASTs. The location is a small object holding the node and the parent path, navigation returns a new location or null at the boundary, and Object.freeze (plus a convention of never writing to shared nodes) stands in for the type-level immutability the language does not have; @thi.ng/zipper is the packaged version of exactly this protocol.
pitfalls: Object.freeze is shallow: a frozen node still exposes a mutable children array, and writes to it fail silently in sloppy mode while module/strict code throws a TypeError.
Spread copies one level only, so [...kids] shares the child objects and a nested write is visible through both versions; structuredClone avoids that but destroys identity and structural sharing.
null sentinels for boundary moves are easy to propagate by accident, turning a failed move into a TypeError two lines later.
Recursion over big trees overflows the stack - iterate with next/prev or an explicit stack when the tree can be deep.

variants.name: @thi.ng/zipper Location (clojure.zip port)
variants.implementation_notes: The packaged form: @thi.ng/zipper (a fork of fast-zip, itself a clojure.zip port) exposes zipper(node, ops, path) and arrayZipper(value) plus a Location with next/prev/left/right/up/down/leftmost/rightmost navigation and remove/replace/update/appendChild/insertChild/insertLeft/insertRight edits, all returning a new Location; the final .root accessor is the single O(depth) zip step. Use it instead of hand-writing the protocol when the tree is JSON-like; the constraint is that the node shape must be described by the branch/children/ factory operations the library expects.
pitfalls: Every verb returns a new Location, so a location kept from before an edit still denotes the old tree - holding several of them keeps whole versions alive.
The Location object is used mutably internally while chaining: calling verbs for their side effect instead of keeping the returned value is the classic mistake.
The ops description must match the node representation exactly; a wrong branch/children pair makes navigation silently skip subtrees instead of failing.
